name: Apachean
region: Arizona, New Mexico, and formerly Texas, Oklahoma and northern Mexico
defining_innovation: Navajo and the Apache languages, the Southern Athabaskans. Navajo is the most widely spoken Native American language in the United States.

chapters.title: Into the Southwest
chapters.body:
The Apachean languages are so close to one another, and so clearly Athabaskan, that their speakers must have reached the Southwest fairly recently, probably around 1300 to 1500 CE. They came either along the eastern edge of the Rockies or through the Great Basin, and the route is still debated. **Harry Hoijer** classified them in 1938 into a western group (Navajo, Western Apache, Chiricahua, Mescalero) and an eastern group (Jicarilla, Lipan, Plains Apache). Plains Apache is now often treated as a separate branch.

Navajo has about 170,000 speakers, more than any other Native language in the United States. During the Second World War, Navajo Code Talkers in the US Marine Corps used it as the basis of a battlefield code that was never broken.

chapters.title: Navajo Today
chapters.body:
Navajo is the only Na-Dene language with a large community of speakers, but it is shrinking. In the mid-20th century most Navajo children arrived at school speaking Navajo; today most grow up speaking English first, and the average age of speakers is rising. The Navajo Nation has responded with its own language policy. Its schools include immersion programmes such as Tséhootsooí Diné Bi'ólta' at Fort Defiance, and Diné College, founded in 1968 as the first tribally controlled college in the United States, teaches the language.

The written standard goes back to the alphabet developed in the 1930s and 1940s and used by Robert Young and William Morgan in their dictionaries. It marks high tone with an acute accent, nasal vowels with a hook, long vowels by doubling, and the glottal stop with an apostrophe, as in *hózhǫ́*, 'beauty, harmony', a central idea in Navajo thought.

The Apache languages are in a weaker position. Western Apache is still spoken on the San Carlos and Fort Apache reservations in Arizona, and Mescalero-Chiricahua and Jicarilla in New Mexico, but mostly by older people. Each nation runs its own teaching programmes, often built on the dictionaries and text collections produced with linguists over the last century.

speakers.note: Nearly all are Navajo speakers, about 160,000 of whom speak it at home; the Apache languages together have a few thousand speakers, most of them Western Apache, and Lipan and Plains Apache are no longer spoken as first languages.

turning_points.title: Arrival in the Southwest
turning_points.description: Apachean speakers arrive in the Southwest from the north, not long before the first Spanish expeditions. The date and route are debated.

sources.citation: Hoijer, Harry. 1938. The southern Athapaskan languages. American Anthropologist 40(1): 75–87.
Mithun, Marianne. 1999. The Languages of Native North America. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

turning_points.title: Writing Navajo
turning_points.description: Robert Young and William Morgan, a Navajo linguist, develop the Latin-based orthography with tone marks and nasal hooks that becomes the standard for Navajo publishing and schooling.

sources.citation: Young, Robert W. & William Morgan Sr. 1987. The Navajo Language: A Grammar and Colloquial Dictionary, rev. ed. Albuquerque: University of New Mexico Press.

turning_points.title: Rough Rock
turning_points.description: The Rough Rock Demonstration School opens on the Navajo Nation, the first school in the United States run by a Native community, teaching in Navajo as well as English.

sources.citation: McCarty, Teresa L. 2002. A Place to Be Navajo: Rough Rock and the Struggle for Self-Determination in Indigenous Schooling. Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum.
